newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - June 17.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - June 17.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. -- NATWEST ISSUES PROFITS WARNING

National Westminster Bank has entered a period of crisis with the resignation of its head of investment banking, Martin Owen, and the issuing of a profits warning. Owen's resignation follows the discovery of mispriced interest rate options in March, which cost the bank 77 million sterling. The bank has also been facing increased pressure of late from shareholders who complain to be receiving inadequate returns from investment banking.
-- SPONSORS OFFERED NEW IMAGE IN BOG ANTS AND SNAILS

UK environment minister Michael Meacher has announced that about 20 companies in the country have expressed interest in supporting deals to protect endangered species. Mecher admits that some of the 116 listed endangered animals have received more interest than others, and now the most difficult task is to find companies that will support some of the "less attractive" animals such as the narrow-headed ant and the depressed river mussel. Supermarket chain Tesco is to sponsor a plan to help preserve the skylark for 100,000 sterling per year.
-- NEW COMPUTER TIMEBOMB THREATENS TO HALT SYSTEMS

With many companies worrying over the effects that the millennium time bomb will have on their business, computer experts have now discovered a new 'timebomb' in older programmes that could disrupt systems in 2000. Experts note that in the '70s, many companies entered 999999 to indicate the end of a project or set of records for processing, a number that translates into the date of 9th September 1999. While the experts say the problem "is not hugely difficult to correct", they note could hit many sectors.
-- BRUSSELS TO PROBE MANCHESTER AIRPORT AID

Further doubt has been cast upon the construction of a second runway at Manchester Airport as the European Commission has announced it is to investigate the legality of a state aid pact to the airport. The Mobberly Parish Council representing 2,750 people affected by the airport development has complained to the EC that most of the 200 million sterling paid by local authorities to the airport has been used as a form of subsidy to reduce charges to airlines to attract business that otherwise may have gone to rival airports.
-- LOTTERY CASH MAY PLUG SPORTS SPONSORSHIP GAP

Government ministers have announced that lottery funding may be used to replace sponsorship funding lost due to the ban on tobacco advertising in sports. While ministers are confident that the new funding will help sports such as cricket, rugby league and golf, they admit less popular sports such as ice hockey and greyhound racing may face problems. A definite announcement into the future of sponsorship is being delayed for fear sports will likewise delay or abandon the search for alternative sponsors.
-- BROADCAST EARNINGS LEAD FIELD ACROSS TELEVISION

A study carried out by the Department of National Heritage has revealed that UK broadcasting generates three times as much revenue as programme production or distribution. The study shows that acquired programming from countries such as the US make the highest contribution of all programmes to broadcasters' gross margins due to the relatively large audiences they attract at low costs. In contrast, public service broadcasting such as children's and religious tends to produce negative financial returns.
-- SOLE BIDDER FOR EMERGENCY RADIO SYSTEM

With the Home Office still trying to encourage multiple bidders for the new nationwide emergency radio system, it appears that the project will go to the sole remaining bidder, Quadrant. The Home Office insists that competition is essential to ensure value for money and have considered the possibility of abandoning the project altogether. Quadrant, a group that includes British Telecommunications, Motorola and TRW, Nokia and two electronics groups from the US, is in negotiations with the Home Office on methods of ensuring it meets tough government standards.
-- UK AND JAPANESE BANKS IN 'BIG BANG' ALLIANCE TALKS

Barclays Bank of the UK is in negotiations with Japan's Hokkaido Takushoku bank over the possibility of an alliance to develop joint asset management and investment services in Japan. The Japanese market will soon experience what has been called a 'big bang' due to a wave of financial deregulation. Andrew Simmonds of Barclays Tokyo said the big bang will 'lead to a lot of new opportunities...and the chance to work with a domestically oriented Japanese group.
-- TIRING REBELS LOSE BATTLE FOR CONTROL

Music company Tiring International has avoided a bid from former directors who had been seeking to take control of it, as chief executive Philip Robinson survived a shareholder vote against those seeking to remove him from his position. The group of rebels was led by Robinson's former friend Mark Frey, who is expected to retain his 11.8 per cent holding in the company as he 'realises the potency of the business'.
-- GRANADA'S 'LAMB' HOPES TO SAFELY GRAZE

A broadcast magazine recently angered James Graham by calling Border Television, the company of which he is managing director, "Granada's pet lamb". Border currently broadcasts to 750,000 viewers on both sides of the Scottish border as well as the Isle of Man and its neighbours, but remains quite small compared to the Granada Group and Scottish Media that are undergoing expansion. Graham s upports Border's size, saying it has tremendous customer support because it emphasises local news more than a national Scottish station would, and that it reported pre-tax profits up 37 percent in the half year to 1.52 million stg.
